analytic_review_groups: The connected compact Hermitian setting and nonzero nonnegative Lp datum with p>1 carry through the continuous equations; the concave sections explicitly change f to an eigenvalue operator and require n>=2.
The comparison reserve is epsilon*omega; torsion inequalities are tested against positive complementary products and nonexistent high degrees are omitted, including dimension one.
Ordered bounded contact controls the complement of a strict sublevel set; decreasing smooth regularization and coefficient convergence justify global integration by parts with the bounded difference.
The five torsion coefficients reduce to k(k-1), k(1+2r), r^2; a<1/32 and q>7/8 make the exact finite induction q^n I0<=In valid.
Strict domination chooses epsilon before the thin height; positive volume and the epsilon^n reserve give a contradiction even when the compared mass on that set is zero.
Every individual bounded potential has positive mass, while a uniform lower bound over the entire bounded class remains a distinct metric hypothesis.
The convex capacity competitor uses tau=t/[2(1-epsilon)(H+1)]; both sublevel inclusions and the inverse comparison factor hold with the declared height.
Backward capacity iteration checks positive levels before applying the inequality; the geometric series leaves a positive limiting level, contradicting positive capacity there.
Capacity-square control of Lp densities and the normalized capacity tail bound the potential depth; bounding the same positive capacity by Cap(X) gives a positive lower density norm.

Normalized L1-Cauchy continuous solutions with uniformly bounded Lp densities become uniformly Cauchy by a fixed epsilon,D argument and Holder/Chebyshev, without assuming convergence of the densities.

Smooth density approximation and Gauduchon AM-GM give a uniform upper scalar bound using nth-root convergence; the lower density norm gives a strictly positive lower scalar bound, with Stokes supplying dimension one.
The extracted scalar and uniform potential limits identify the bounded Bedford–Taylor measure; existence does not require invariant mass or a metric-wide lower volume property.

For the exponential equation, Jensen uses the probability weighted by the nth root of the density; Holder pairs its L(np) norm with normalized potentials in L(np/(np-1)), and the lower density norm controls the additive constant.

Bounded exponential comparison proves the reversed density order and uniqueness where the density vanishes; applying it to exp(-u)*f proves continuity of any bounded Lp solution without a circular continuity premise.

Constant translates of one continuous scalar solution bracket the unique positive-exponent solution; multiplying by lambda gives the logarithmic scalar limit and uniqueness of the scalar, but not uniqueness of a normalized potential cluster.
The C2 scalar comparison adds epsilon*omega at a maximum of u-(1+epsilon)v; this makes the second form positive at the comparison point before dividing determinants.
The Hopf threefold mass is 6*c_f*I_f, and the preceding fibre energy inequality gives exactly the L2 defect bound with factor 4.

Equality descends a bounded potential through local holomorphic sections; the a.e. density is treated as an invariant measure, and Haar averaging yields an a.e. base density rather than unsupported pointwise invariance.
Jensen gives the base Lp bound; the closed base equation has scalar I_f^-1, and decreasing bounded products with the vertical beta restriction 2*dA_E yield the exact total-space cube identity.

Near equality combines uniform potential compactness with reflexive weak Lp density compactness; equality identifies each subsequential limit and self-adjoint Haar averaging proves the whole weak defect convergence.

The oscillating radial example has positive coefficients, exact mean 1+a^2/(2*pi^2*m^2), uniform potential defect tending to zero and density L1 defect tending to 2a/pi, so weak convergence cannot be strengthened here.
Each concave asymptotic function is finite continuous everywhere or infinite everywhere; compactness of the reference eigenvalues permits a common positive shift and continuous upper level H.
An unbounded positive matrix perturbation forces an ordered eigenvalue to diverge; the fixed-coordinate monotonicity comparison contradicts the common strict asymptotic gap.
The concave C0 argument uses a fixed trace Green bound and a real contact set; the strict-gap matrix bound controls its nonnegative real Hessian trace and hence gives positive contact volume.

The auxiliary Monge–Ampere cutoff density has lower bound 1/2, unit average and common L2 bound; the choices of kappa,M,epsilon0 are ordered before the cutoff, giving uniform scalar/potential constants independent of cutoff derivatives.
At the weighted-difference maximum, concavity bounds the positive perturbation above by R, while the cutoff auxiliary determinant forces it above R^n; interchanging solutions yields linear stability.
The Gauduchon-weighted product rule and 0<=u<=C give a W1,2 bound; Rellich, right-hand-side equicontinuity and linear stability yield C0 precompactness and a common modulus.

Concavity and positivity along cone rays give nonnegative dual traces and a lower positive trace T; the common strict-gap tangent-hyperplane alternative has constants independent of the positive level.

Connectedness of the compact coordinate upper set handles a tangent plane missing it; otherwise shifted coordinate tests bound every normal component below, and opposite eigenvalue/derivative orders justify the matrix rearrangement inequality.

The Chern commutation errors retain nonsymmetric pure derivatives; half the mixed Hessian square absorbs torsion, and completing the weighted pure square leaves the displayed lambda and chi cross terms.

The nearby comparison radius is chosen after a and beta, independently of derivatives of V; explicit Young bounds give a positive weighted-gradient bracket in both linearized alternatives and a uniform oscillation of the weight.

C0 compactness supplies a finite net of smooth admissible solutions, whose finitely many gradients control the family; the final gradient estimate retains the strict reference gap and the bound for the right-hand-side derivative.
